newsitem.title: GEORGIA: Abkhaz leader says no to new talks with Georgia.
newsitem.headline: Abkhaz leader says no to new talks with Georgia.

text.p: The leader of Georgia's breakaway region of Abkhazia spat defiance at Tbilisi on Thursday and said severed phone lines to his region would not force him back to the negotiating table.
"With the economic blockade from Russia and now the cutting off of phone links, any talks with Georgia would be impossible," Interfax news agency quoted Abkhaz leader Vladislav Ardzinba as saying.
Russia severed its last 48 inter-city phone lines with Abkhazia this week and officials in Tbilisi said the Black Sea region could hook up to the Georgian phone grid.

Georgia had insisted upon the measure as part of a campaign of sanctions aimed at bringing Abkhazia to heel. Abkhazia retaliated by cutting power supplies from a massive hydro-electric power station on the river between the regions.
The Abkhaz, who routed Georgian troops in a year of fighting from 1992-93, have refused to hook up to the Georgian grid, and they say the cable to Georgia is damaged.

Now the region, home to an estimated 200,000 people out of a prewar population of 550,000, has no regular phone links to the outside world, although separatist government officials are believed to have a small number of portable satellite phones.
Ardzinba said the telephone cutoff was a political move which showed Russia was trying to "chase us into Georgia".

Abkhazia, once a thriving beach playland for the Soviet communist elite, is an eerie relic of its former self after more than a year of sanctions imposed by the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) and enforced by Russia.

Imports and exports into the lush palm-fringed land are strictly limited and tourists, once the mainstay of the economy, are not allowed in. The loss of phone links is sure to deepen its sense of isolation.

Abkhazia has enjoyed de facto independence since the fighting with Georgia ended, but it has not been recognised as an independent state. More than 150,000 ethnic Georgians, once nearly half the population, fled Abkhazia and cannot return.
Moscow gave the Abkhaz military help during the conflict, but it now generally supports Georgia. It has separatist problems of its own in nearby Chechnya.
Peace talks are deadlocked, with Georgia offering only autonomy in a federal state and the Abkhaz insisting upon either legal or de facto independence in a loose confederation.
